screens.title: DLL Hijacking & Search Order Hijacking
screens.subtitle: Exploiting Windows Dynamic Link Library Loading Mechanisms

narration.text: Welcome to a critical chapter in advanced exploitation: DLL Hijacking and Search Order Hijacking. In the world of Windows operating systems, Dynamic Link Libraries, or DLLs, are fundamental components. They are shared libraries of code and resources that applications use to perform common functions, making software development efficient. However, this essential mechanism can be a powerful attack vector. If an attacker can manipulate how an application loads its required DLLs, they can inject and execute their own malicious code, often leading to significant privilege escalation or persistence on a compromised system. This chapter will demystify the DLL loading process, show you how to identify vulnerabilities, and guide you through crafting and deploying your own malicious DLLs to achieve your exploitation goals. Understanding this technique is crucial for any aspiring penetration tester or red team operator, as it reveals a common, yet often overlooked, pathway to system control.

keyIdea.title: Control the Flow
keyIdea.text: DLL Hijacking allows attackers to control program execution by manipulating how applications load shared libraries.

screens.title: Understanding DLL Loading
screens.subtitle: How Windows Applications Find Dynamic Link Libraries

narration.text: Dynamic Link Libraries, or DLLs, are essentially shared code modules that Windows applications use to perform common functions. Think of them as specialized toolboxes that multiple programs can access, rather than each program carrying its own set of tools. When an application needs a specific function, it doesn't embed that function directly into its own executable; instead, it calls upon a DLL. This approach saves memory, reduces disk space, and allows for easier updates, as a single DLL update can benefit all applications that use it. The crucial part for us is how Windows locates these DLLs. When an application starts and requires a DLL, the operating system initiates a search process. This search isn't random; it follows a predefined sequence of directories, known as the DLL search order. Understanding this mechanism is the bedrock of comprehending DLL hijacking, as it reveals the exact points where an attacker can interject their own malicious code. If we can predict or influence where Windows looks for a DLL, we can trick an application into loading our version instead of the legitimate one. This is the fundamental principle we will exploit.

keyIdea.title: Shared Code, Shared Vulnerability
keyIdea.text: DLLs are shared code, and their loading mechanism presents a critical attack surface if the search order is manipulated.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.7›Understanding DLL Loading
Core Concept

Understanding DLL Loading

How Windows Applications Find Dynamic Link Libraries

The Role of DLLs

  • •Shared Code: DLLs contain functions and resources used by multiple applications, promoting code reuse.
  • •Memory Efficiency: Reduces memory footprint as code is loaded once and shared across processes.
  • •Modularity: Allows for easier updates and maintenance, as components can be replaced independently.
  • •Dynamic Linking: Applications link to DLLs at runtime, not compile time, offering flexibility.
Key Takeaway

The DLL loading mechanism is a core Windows function, and its predictable search order is the foundation for hijacking attacks.

DLL Loading Process

1. Application Starts

Requires a specific function or resource.

2. Windows Initiates Search

Follows a predefined 'DLL Search Order'.

3. DLL Found & Loaded

Application executes functions from the loaded DLL.

Analogy

Imagine a chef needing a specific ingredient. Instead of always having it on hand, they check a list of places in a specific order (pantry, then local market, then specialty store). If an attacker can put a fake ingredient in the pantry, the chef uses that first.

screens.title: The Windows DLL Search Order
screens.subtitle: The Specific Sequence of Directories Windows Checks

narration.text: When an application needs to load a DLL, Windows doesn't just randomly look for it. It follows a very specific, predefined sequence of directories. This sequence, known as the DLL search order, is crucial because it dictates where an application will first attempt to find a required library. The default order typically starts with the directory where the application itself was loaded from. This makes sense, as many applications keep their essential DLLs alongside their executable. Next, it checks the system directories, like System32 and System, which house core Windows components. Following these, it looks in the main Windows directory. Importantly, the current directory is also part of this search path, which can sometimes be exploited if a user has write permissions there. Finally, Windows checks the directories listed in the system's PATH environment variable. While this order can vary slightly based on Windows versions or specific safe DLL search mode settings, the general principle remains: a predictable sequence. Attackers leverage this predictability. If they can place a malicious DLL in an earlier-searched directory than the legitimate one, or if the legitimate DLL is missing and they can place their malicious version in any of the searched directories, their code will be executed. This systematic approach to finding DLLs is both a convenience for developers and a significant vulnerability for security.

keyIdea.title: Predictable Path, Exploitable Weakness
keyIdea.text: The fixed DLL search order provides a predictable path for Windows to find libraries, which attackers can exploit by inserting malicious DLLs earlier in the sequence.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.7›DLL Search Order
Process Flow

The Windows DLL Search Order

The Specific Sequence of Directories Windows Checks

Default Search Sequence

  • •Application Directory: The folder where the executable itself resides.
  • •System Directory: Typically %SystemRoot%\System32.
  • •16-bit System Directory: Usually %SystemRoot%\System.
  • •Windows Directory: The main %SystemRoot% folder.
  • •Current Directory: The directory from which the application was launched.
  • •PATH Environment Variable: Directories listed in the system's PATH.
Key Takeaway

The predictable nature of the DLL search order is a fundamental aspect that attackers exploit to inject malicious code.

screens.title: What is DLL Hijacking?
screens.subtitle: Exploiting the DLL Loading Mechanism for Code Execution

narration.text: DLL Hijacking, also known as DLL Search Order Hijacking, is a sophisticated attack technique that exploits the very mechanism we just discussed: the Windows DLL search order. The core idea is to trick a legitimate application into loading a malicious DLL instead of its intended, benign counterpart. This can happen in a couple of primary ways. First, if an application attempts to load a DLL that is simply missing from the system, an attacker can place their malicious DLL in one of the directories that Windows searches. Since the legitimate DLL isn't found, the operating system will eventually find and load the attacker's version. Second, even if the legitimate DLL exists, an attacker might be able to place their malicious DLL in a directory that is searched *earlier* in the sequence. Because Windows stops searching once it finds a DLL with the requested name, the malicious DLL will be loaded first, effectively 'hijacking' the process. The impact of this attack can be severe. If a high-privileged application, such as one running as Administrator or SYSTEM, falls victim to DLL hijacking, the attacker's code will execute with those elevated privileges, granting them significant control over the system. This makes DLL hijacking a prime technique for privilege escalation and maintaining persistence on a target machine. It's a silent, yet incredibly powerful, way to subvert trust in the operating system's fundamental processes.

keyIdea.title: Malicious Substitution
keyIdea.text: DLL Hijacking involves substituting a legitimate DLL with a malicious one, leveraging the search order to execute attacker-controlled code.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.7›What is DLL Hijacking?
Attack Vector

What is DLL Hijacking?

Exploiting the DLL Loading Mechanism for Code Execution

Core Principles of Hijacking

  • •Missing DLLs: An application requests a DLL that doesn't exist; attacker provides a malicious one.
  • •Insecure Search Paths: Attacker places a malicious DLL in a directory searched before the legitimate one.
  • •Privilege Escalation: If the vulnerable application runs with high privileges, the malicious DLL inherits them.
  • •Persistence: Can be used to maintain access by ensuring malicious code runs on application startup.
Key Takeaway

DLL Hijacking is a powerful technique to execute arbitrary code with elevated privileges by manipulating the Windows DLL search order.

Hijacking Scenarios

Missing DLL

Application requests a DLL that doesn't exist.

Insecure Path

Malicious DLL placed in an earlier-searched, writable directory.

Example

A SYSTEM process launches from C:\ProgramData\App\ and tries to load missing.dll. If a low-privileged user has write permissions to C:\ProgramData\App\, they can place their malicious missing.dll there, leading to SYSTEM privilege execution.

narration.text: The key to successful DLL hijacking lies in identifying the right target: a vulnerable process. Not all applications are equally susceptible, and we're particularly interested in those running with high privileges, such as Administrator or SYSTEM. These are the processes whose compromise offers the greatest reward in terms of privilege escalation. A process becomes vulnerable when it attempts to load a DLL that is either missing entirely or is searched for in a directory where a low-privileged user has write permissions. Consider a scenario where a SYSTEM process is launched from a directory like 'C:\ProgramData\App\'. If this process then tries to load a DLL, say 'missing. dll', and that DLL doesn't exist, Windows will proceed through its search order. If a low-privileged user has write permissions to 'C:\ProgramData\App\', they can simply place their malicious 'missing. dll' in that directory. When the SYSTEM process starts, it will find and load the attacker's DLL first, executing the malicious code with SYSTEM privileges. This combination of a high-privileged process, a missing DLL, and weak directory permissions creates a perfect storm for a DLL hijacking attack. Our goal is to systematically uncover these specific conditions on a target system.

keyIdea.title: Privilege + Path + Missing DLL
keyIdea.text: Vulnerable processes combine high privileges, a missing DLL, and a writable search path, creating an opportunity for privilege escalation.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.7›Vulnerable Processes
Vulnerability Analysis

Identifying Vulnerable Processes

When High-Privilege Applications Become Targets

Key Vulnerability Conditions

  • •High-Privilege Process: The target application runs as Administrator or SYSTEM.
  • •Missing DLL: The application attempts to load a DLL that does not exist.
  • •Insecure Write Permissions: A low-privileged user has write access to a directory in the DLL search path.
  • •Predictable Search Order: The application's DLL loading behavior is consistent and exploitable.
Key Takeaway

The convergence of high privileges, missing DLLs, and writable search paths creates prime DLL hijacking opportunities.

Vulnerability Chain

1. High-Privilege App

e.g., SYSTEM process

2. Attempts to Load DLL

e.g., missing.dll

3. DLL is Missing / Insecure Path

Low-priv user can write to search path.

4. Attacker Places Malicious DLL

Code executes with high privileges.

Scenario

A scheduled task runs C:\App\service.exe as SYSTEM. service.exe tries to load utility.dll from its own directory, but utility.dll is absent. If a standard user can write to C:\App\, they can plant a malicious utility.dll.

screens.title: Discovering Missing DLLs with Procmon
screens.subtitle: Real-time Monitoring for 'NAME NOT FOUND' Events

narration.text: Identifying DLL hijacking opportunities requires a powerful diagnostic tool, and for Windows, that tool is Process Monitor, or Procmon, from Sysinternals. Procmon allows you to monitor file system, Registry, and process activity in real-time, providing an unparalleled view into how applications interact with the operating system. To find missing DLLs, we'll configure Procmon with specific filters. First, we'll narrow down the events to a target process, typically one running with elevated privileges. Then, we'll filter for 'CreateFile' operations, as this is the action Windows performs when attempting to load a DLL. The most crucial filter is 'Result is NAME NOT FOUND'. This tells Procmon to show us only those instances where an application tried to access a file, but the file simply wasn't there. Finally, we'll ensure the path ends with '. dll' to focus specifically on Dynamic Link Libraries. Once these filters are set, you start the target application, and Procmon will reveal any missing DLLs that the process attempts to load. The 'Path' column in Procmon's output will show you exactly where the application was looking for the DLL, which is vital for determining if that location is writable by a low-privileged user. This systematic approach with Procmon is the most effective way to pinpoint DLL load failures that can be exploited.

keyIdea.title: Procmon's Precision
keyIdea.text: Process Monitor, with specific filters, precisely identifies missing DLLs by capturing 'NAME NOT FOUND' events during application execution.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.7›Procmon Discovery
Tooling & Discovery

Discovering Missing DLLs with Procmon

Real-time Monitoring for 'NAME NOT FOUND' Events

Procmon Filter Criteria

  • •Process Name: Target the specific high-privileged application (e.g., TargetProcess.exe).
  • •Operation: Filter for CreateFile, indicating an attempt to open or create a file.
  • •Result: Crucially, look for NAME NOT FOUND, signifying a failed file lookup.
  • •Path: Ensure the path ends with .dll to focus on Dynamic Link Libraries.
Key Takeaway

Procmon's precise filtering capabilities are indispensable for identifying missing DLLs and the exact paths where applications search for them.

# Example of using Process Monitor (Procmon)
# 1. Start Procmon.
# 2. Set filters:
- Process Name is <TargetProcess.exe>
- Operation is 'CreateFile'
- Result is 'NAME NOT FOUND'
- Path ends with '.dll'
# 3. Start the target high-privileged application.
# 4. Observe missing DLLs.
Pro Tip

Always run Procmon as an administrator to ensure it captures all system-level events, especially those related to high-privileged processes.

narration.text: Beyond just finding missing DLLs, another critical aspect of DLL hijacking reconnaissance is identifying insecure load paths. This means finding directories within the DLL search order that are writable by a low-privileged user. Even if a DLL isn't missing, if an attacker can place their malicious DLL in a directory that is searched *before* the legitimate one, and they have write permissions to that directory, they can still hijack the loading process. A useful command-line tool for this is wmic, the Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line utility. By using wmic process get Executable Path,Command Line, you can enumerate the full paths of all running processes and their command lines. This output helps you understand where applications are being launched from. Once you have these paths, you can then manually or programmatically check the permissions on those directories. If a high-privileged process is launched from a directory that a low-privileged user can write to, it presents a significant opportunity. For instance, if a service running as SYSTEM executes an application from C. backslash Program Data backslash My App backslash, and a standard user has write access to C. backslash Program Data backslash My App backslash, that directory becomes a prime candidate for placing a malicious DLL. This step complements Procmon's findings by helping you assess the writeability of potential DLL drop zones.

keyIdea.title: Path to Privilege
keyIdea.text: Identifying writable directories in a high-privileged process's search path is crucial for placing malicious DLLs and achieving privilege escalation.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.7›Insecure Paths
Reconnaissance

Identifying Insecure Load Paths

Using wmic to Find Writable Directories

Why Insecure Paths Matter

  • •Precedence: If a malicious DLL is placed in an earlier-searched, writable directory, it will be loaded first.
  • •Low-Privilege Write: A standard user can drop a malicious DLL into a directory used by a high-privileged process.
  • •Common Vulnerability: Often found in poorly configured application installations or custom services.
Key Takeaway

Combining process path enumeration with permission checks reveals critical insecure load paths for DLL hijacking.

# Enumerate process paths to identify potential vulnerable directories
wmic process get ExecutablePath,CommandLine
ExecutablePath CommandLine
C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe -k LocalServiceNetworkRestricted
C:\Program Files\VendorApp\app.exe "C:\Program Files\VendorApp\app.exe" -start
C:\ProgramData\CustomService\service.exe C:\ProgramData\CustomService\service.exe
Actionable Insight

After identifying paths, use tools like icacls or accesschk to verify if low-privileged users have write permissions to these directories.

screens.title: Crafting a Malicious DLL
screens.subtitle: Developing a Custom DLL for Code Execution

narration.text: Once you've identified a vulnerable process and a missing or insecurely loaded DLL, the next step is to craft your malicious DLL. This involves writing code that will execute your desired payload when the DLL is loaded by the target application. The core of any DLL is its Dll Main function. This special entry point is executed by the operating system at various stages of a DLL's lifecycle, most importantly when the DLL is attached to a process, indicated by DLL underscore PROCESS underscore ATTACH. This is where you'll place your malicious code. For simplicity and proof-of-concept, a DLL that merely spawns a Message Box with a message like 'DLL Hijacked!' is often sufficient to demonstrate the vulnerability. For more advanced exploitation, you would embed a reverse shell payload, allowing you to gain remote control over the compromised system. The key is to ensure your DLL is correctly structured to be loaded by Windows. If you are replacing an *existing* DLL, your malicious DLL might also need to export the same functions as the legitimate one to prevent the application from crashing. However, for a *missing* DLL, this is less of a concern, as the application isn't expecting specific functions from it. The provided C code snippet illustrates a basic structure for a malicious DLL, ready to be compiled into your payload.

keyIdea.title: Code Injection via DllMain
keyIdea.text: Crafting a malicious DLL involves embedding a payload within the `DllMain` function, which executes when the DLL is loaded by a vulnerable process.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.7›Crafting Malicious DLL
Payload Development

Crafting a Malicious DLL

Developing a Custom DLL for Code Execution

Key Elements of a Malicious DLL

  • •DllMain Function: The entry point where your malicious code will be executed.
  • •DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH: The specific reason for call to trigger your payload when the DLL is loaded.
  • •Payload: Can be a simple MessageBox for PoC or a full reverse shell.
  • •Function Exports (Optional): If replacing an existing DLL, ensure your DLL exports the same functions.
Key Takeaway

The DllMain function, specifically during DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH, is the primary location to embed and execute malicious code within a custom DLL.

// malicious.c (for a simple reverse shell or MessageBox)
#include <windows.h>
#include <stdio.h>
// Function to be called when the DLL is loaded
BOOL APIENTRY DllMain(HMODULE hModule, DWORD ul_reason_for_call, LPVOID lpReserved) {
switch (ul_reason_for_call) {
case DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH:
// Your malicious code here
// Example: MessageBox(NULL, "DLL Hijacked!", "Pwned", MB_OK);
// Example: Call a function to spawn a reverse shell
break;
case DLL_THREAD_ATTACH:
case DLL_THREAD_DETACH:
case DLL_PROCESS_DETACH:
break;
}
return TRUE;
}
Consideration

For a missing DLL, you generally don't need to worry about exporting specific functions. For replacing an existing DLL, you might need to replicate its exports to avoid application crashes.

narration.text: After writing your malicious C code for the DLL, the next crucial step is to compile it into a functional Dynamic Link Library file. For cross-compilation, especially when targeting Windows from a Linux environment like Kali, mingw32-gcc is an invaluable tool. This GCC-based cross-compiler allows you to generate Windows executables and DLLs. The command to compile your C source file, for example malicious. c, into a DLL is straightforward but requires specific flags. You'll use x86 underscore 64-w64-mingw32-gcc for 64-bit Windows targets. The -shared flag is essential; it tells the compiler to create a shared library, which is what a DLL fundamentally is. You'll also specify your source file, malicious. c, and finally, the output file name using the -o flag, ensuring it ends with the. dll extension, such as missing. dll. This output name should match the name of the DLL you intend to hijack. For instance, if the vulnerable application is looking for utility. dll, your compiled malicious DLL should also be named utility. dll. Once compiled, you'll have a. dll file ready to be transferred to the target Windows system. This compiled DLL is the weapon you'll deploy to achieve your exploitation goals, so ensuring it's correctly built is paramount.

keyIdea.title: Cross-Compilation Power
keyIdea.text: `mingw32-gcc` enables cross-compilation of C code into Windows DLLs from Linux, a key step in preparing malicious payloads.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.7›Compiling DLL
Payload Compilation

Compiling the Malicious DLL

Using mingw32-gcc to Create Your Payload

Compilation Steps & Flags

  • •Compiler: Use x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc for 64-bit Windows targets from Kali.
  • •-shared Flag: Essential for creating a shared library (DLL) instead of an executable.
  • •Input File: Specify your C source code file (e.g., malicious.c).
  • •Output File: Use -o to define the output DLL name (e.g., missing.dll), matching the target DLL.
Key Takeaway

Correctly compiling your C code into a DLL using mingw32-gcc with the -shared flag is a critical step in preparing your DLL hijacking payload.

# Compile malicious.c into a DLL named missing.dll
x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc -shared malicious.c -o missing.dll
# Example output (success)
# (No output usually means success)
# Verify the file type
file missing.dll
missing.dll: PE32+ executable (DLL) (console) x86-64, for MS Windows
Important Note

Ensure the compiled DLL's architecture (x86 or x64) matches that of the target vulnerable application to avoid loading failures.

screens.title: Executing the DLL Hijack
screens.subtitle: Transferring and Triggering Your Malicious Payload

narration.text: With your malicious DLL successfully compiled, it's time to execute the DLL hijack. This process involves three distinct, yet interconnected, steps. First, you need to transfer your crafted DLL to the target system. This can be done through various methods, such as a web server, SMB share, or by exploiting existing file transfer capabilities on the target. The critical aspect here is placing the DLL in the *vulnerable directory* you identified earlier – the one that is searched by the high-privileged application and is writable by your current low-privileged user. Once the malicious DLL is in place, the second step is to trigger the vulnerable process. This means starting or restarting the high-privileged application that attempts to load the DLL you've hijacked. This could involve restarting a service, waiting for a scheduled task to run, or simply launching the application if you have the necessary permissions. As soon as the application starts, Windows will follow its DLL search order, find your malicious DLL in the vulnerable directory, and load it. At this point, your embedded payload, whether it's a simple message box or a reverse shell, will execute with the privileges of the compromised application. This final stage is where you observe the fruits of your reconnaissance and payload development, gaining the desired access or control.

keyIdea.title: Deploy, Trigger, Execute
keyIdea.text: Executing a DLL hijack involves transferring the malicious DLL to a vulnerable path, then triggering the target process to load and execute the payload.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.7›Executing Hijack
Attack Execution

Executing the DLL Hijack

Transferring and Triggering Your Malicious Payload

The Three-Step Exploitation

  • •Create Malicious DLL: Develop your custom DLL with the desired payload (covered in previous screens).
  • •Transfer DLL: Place your crafted DLL into the identified vulnerable directory on the target system.
  • •Trigger Process: Start or restart the high-privileged application that will load your malicious DLL.
Key Takeaway

Successful DLL hijacking relies on precise placement of the malicious DLL and correctly triggering the vulnerable high-privileged process.

Exploitation Flow

01

Malicious DLL Ready

02

Transfer to Vulnerable Path

03

Trigger Vulnerable Process

04

Payload Executes

Example Scenario

After compiling missing.dll, you transfer it to C:\VulnerableApp\. You then restart the legit.exe service, which loads your DLL, granting you a SYSTEM shell on your Kali listener.

narration.text: As with any advanced exploitation technique, DLL hijacking comes with its own set of common pitfalls that can lead to application crashes or failed exploits. One of the most frequent mistakes, especially when attempting to replace an *existing* legitimate DLL, is not ensuring that your malicious DLL exports the same functions. If the target application tries to call a specific function from the hijacked DLL and that function isn't present, the application will likely crash, alerting administrators and potentially losing your foothold. For missing DLLs, this is less of a concern, as the application isn't expecting any specific exports. Another critical consideration is the architecture of your DLL. Ensure that your compiled malicious DLL, whether 32-bit or 64-bit, matches the architecture of the target application. An architecture mismatch will prevent the DLL from loading correctly. Furthermore, always exercise extreme caution and only perform DLL hijacking in controlled lab environments. These techniques can cause significant application instability, system crashes, and unintended side effects in production systems. Thorough testing in a safe sandbox is paramount. By being mindful of these common mistakes and adhering to best practices, you can increase the reliability and effectiveness of your DLL hijacking attempts while minimizing unwanted disruptions.

keyIdea.title: Precision and Caution
keyIdea.text: Successful DLL hijacking requires precise function exports (for existing DLLs), matching architectures, and strict adherence to lab environments to prevent crashes.

content.html:
Module 8›Chapter 8.7›Avoiding Pitfalls
Best Practices

Avoiding Common DLL Hijacking Pitfalls

Ensuring Stability and Effective Exploitation

Critical Considerations

  • •Function Exports: If replacing an existing DLL, ensure your malicious DLL exports all expected functions to prevent crashes.
  • •Architecture Match: The DLL's architecture (x86/x64) must match the target application's architecture.
  • •Controlled Environment: Always perform DLL hijacking in isolated lab environments to avoid system instability.
  • •Thorough Testing: Test your malicious DLL extensively in a safe environment before attempting on a target.
Key Takeaway

Careful attention to DLL exports, architecture, and responsible lab-only execution is vital for successful and stable DLL hijacking.

Common Mistakes & Solutions

Missing Exports

Application crashes if expected functions are not found.

Solution: Replicate Exports

Use tools like dumpbin /exports to identify and replicate legitimate DLL exports.

Architecture Mismatch

32-bit DLL loaded by 64-bit app (or vice-versa) fails.

Solution: Match Architecture

Compile your DLL to match the target application's architecture (x86 or x64).

Safety Note

DLL hijacking can cause application instability or crashes. Always exercise extreme caution and only perform these techniques in controlled lab environments.

narration.text: As we conclude this chapter on DLL Hijacking, let's reinforce the fundamental concepts that underpin this powerful exploitation technique. First, remember that a DLL, or Dynamic Link Library, is a shared library of code and resources vital for Windows applications. It's the building block that many programs rely on. Second, the DLL Search Order is the precise sequence of directories Windows checks when trying to locate and load a DLL. This predictable order is the very vulnerability we exploit. Third, DLL Hijacking itself is the attack where a malicious DLL is strategically placed in a directory searched by a legitimate application before its intended DLL, causing the malicious version to be loaded and executed instead. These three concepts form the core understanding required to identify and execute DLL hijacking attacks. Grasping their interplay is crucial for any aspiring penetration tester, as it unlocks a significant avenue for privilege escalation and persistence on Windows systems. Keep these definitions clear in your mind as you move forward.

keyIdea.text: DLLs, their search order, and the hijacking mechanism are foundational for understanding this Windows exploitation technique.

Module 8›Chapter 8.7›Key Concepts

Key Concepts

Essential Terms to Remember

DLL (Dynamic Link Library)

A shared library of code and resources used by Windows applications to perform common functions.

DLL Search Order

The specific sequence of directories that Windows checks when attempting to locate and load a DLL.

DLL Hijacking

An attack where a malicious DLL is placed in a directory searched by a legitimate application before its intended DLL, causing the malicious DLL to be loaded and executed instead.

Summary Takeaway

DLLs are fundamental to Windows, and their predictable search order creates a powerful attack surface for code injection and privilege escalation.

narration.text: Let's continue our review of key concepts by focusing on the practical tools and functions essential for DLL hijacking. First, Process Monitor, or Procmon, is an indispensable Sysinternals tool. It allows you to monitor file system, Registry, and process activity in real-time, making it invaluable for identifying DLL load failures, specifically those 'NAME NOT FOUND' events. Second, Dll Main is the critical entry point function for a DLL. This is where your malicious code resides, executing when the DLL is loaded or unloaded by a process. Understanding its role is key to crafting effective payloads. Finally, 'NAME NOT FOUND' is a common error message you'll encounter in Procmon, indicating that a file, often a DLL, could not be located in the specified search path. This specific result is your primary indicator of a potential DLL hijacking vulnerability. These tools and concepts are your practical arsenal for discovering and exploiting DLL hijacking opportunities. Mastering them will significantly enhance your ability to perform advanced reconnaissance and develop targeted exploits on Windows systems.

keyIdea.text: Procmon, `DllMain`, and 'NAME NOT FOUND' are the essential tools and indicators for practical DLL hijacking discovery and payload execution.

Key Concepts

Tools and Functions for Exploitation

Process Monitor (Procmon)

A Sysinternals tool used to monitor file system, Registry, and process/thread activity in real-time, invaluable for identifying DLL load failures.

DllMain

The entry point function for a DLL, executed when the DLL is loaded or unloaded by a process, ideal for embedding malicious code.

A common error message in Process Monitor indicating that a file (often a DLL) could not be located in the specified search path, signaling a potential vulnerability.

Summary Takeaway

Leveraging Procmon to find NAME NOT FOUND events and understanding DllMain are critical for successful DLL hijacking exploitation.
